sections.heading: SFTP servers
sections.text: The first download from an SFTP server stops before logging in and asks Trust this server?, with the server's key fingerprint (SHA256:…). Nothing has been sent yet: no login, no file name. Check the fingerprint with the server's owner before trusting it. On the server, ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub prints it. Choose Trust and continue only if they match. Cancel leaves the download failed. Retry connects again and asks again. If you close Apollo Download Manager without answering, it doesn't ask at the next start: Retry the download to see the question again. "The server's host key changed" means the server shows another key than the one you trusted. A reinstalled server does that, and so does an attacker. Apollo Download Manager refuses it every time. Ask the server's owner whether and why the key changed (Troubleshooting).

sections.heading: Files and folders
sections.text: No file is ever overwritten. If a file appears at a download's name while it downloads, from V1 or any other program, Apollo Download Manager keeps it and stops the download: "the destination file already exists; it is never replaced". While downloading, the data goes to <name>.vdmpart beside the final file, which gets its name only once the download is complete and, with a checksum, verified. Look-alike names: two names that look the same but are typed differently are two files. On Windows, names that differ only in upper and lower case are the same file. Long paths: downloads into folders deeper than Windows' old 260-character limit work. Marked as from the internet (Windows): a finished direct download is marked as downloaded from the internet, as browsers mark theirs, so Windows SmartScreen and Office still warn before opening it. The mark names only the server (for example https://example.com/), never the rest of the link. On a drive that can't hold the mark, such as a FAT32 or exFAT USB stick, the download finishes without it. A finished torrent's files are marked too, without a server, since a torrent has none. Delete files removes only that download's own file and its unfinished part, inside its folder. A link in their place (a symbolic link or a junction) is never followed, and what it points to is never touched. Cloud-sync folders such as OneDrive work as ordinary folders.

Apollo Download Manager never writes them to its database, its saved progress or its log. Remember this login in the system keychain, in the Add dialog and the login window, is off by default. Ticked, the download's login is kept in Windows Credential Manager or the Secret Service on Linux (GNOME Keyring, KWallet), and removing the download deletes it there. When the server refuses the login: the window Log in to download opens, says the server refused it, and asks for the user name and password (and, for SFTP, the key). sections.heading: Direct downloads
sections.text: Protocol Links Several connections Resumes Resume checked against the file HTTP/2 Encrypted HTTP and HTTPS http://, https:// Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes FTP and FTPS ftp://, ftps:// No Yes Yes No Yes SFTP sftp:// No Yes Yes No Yes What the columns mean: Several connections: Apollo Download Manager splits the file and downloads its parts over several connections at once. It starts with all the connections a download may use (8 by default) and keeps only those that make it faster. FTP and SFTP use one connection per download for now. Resumes: a paused download, or one interrupted by a restart, a crash or a power cut, goes on from the last progress Apollo Download Manager saved, not from the start. Resume checked against the file: before resuming, Apollo Download Manager checks the file on the server is still the same one (its ETag or modification time). If it changed, Apollo Download Manager starts over rather than mix two versions. HTTP/2: with a server that speaks HTTP/2, several parts share one connection. Apollo Download Manager tries separate connections too, and keeps whichever is faster. Encrypted: HTTPS: always, and the server's certificate is always checked. There is no way to turn that check off. FTP: an ftps:// link is encrypted. A plain ftp:// link is encrypted only when you tick "Require encryption (FTPS)" when adding it. Without that, the Add dialog warns that the login and the file can be read on the network. SFTP: always. The first time you download from a server, Apollo Download Manager asks you to confirm the server's identity (Downloads).
